qs.q: A tree contains 25 nodes. How many edges does it have?
qs.e: Every node except the root has exactly one edge to its parent, so a tree with n nodes always has $n - 1$ edges: $25 - 1 = $ <mark>24</mark>.

qs.q: Consider this tree (parent → children): `A` → `B`, `C` `C` → `D`, `E`, `F` All other nodes are leaves. What are the degree of node A and the degree of the tree?

c.x: Degree of `A` is 3; degree of the tree is 3
Degree of `A` is 2; degree of the tree is 3
Degree of `A` is 2; degree of the tree is 2
Degree of `A` is 3; degree of the tree is 2

e: The degree of a node is its number of children: `A` has 2 children (`B`, `C`), so degree(`A`) = 2.
`C` has 3 children (`D`, `E`, `F`), so degree(`C`) = 3.
The degree of a tree is the <u>maximum</u> degree of any node, which is 3.
<mark>Degree of A = 2; degree of the tree = 3</mark>

qs.q:
Consider this tree (parent → left child, right child):
`A` → `B`, `C`
`B` → `D`, `E`
`E` → `F`, `G`
All other nodes are leaves.
Which set contains <u>all</u> the ancestors of node `G`?
qs.e: Ancestors are the nodes above a node on its path to the root. The path to `G` is `A` → `B` → `E` → `G`, so its ancestors are <mark>E, B, A</mark> (not `G` itself, and not its sibling `F`).

qs.q: Consider this tree (parent → children): `A` → `B`, `C` `B` → `D` `D` → `E` All other nodes are leaves. What is the height of this tree (root at level 0, height counted in edges)?
e: The height is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf.
The longest path is `A` → `B` → `D` → `E`, which has 3 edges.
The other path `A` → `C` has only 1 edge.
<mark>Height = 3</mark>

qs.q: In a binary tree whose root is at level 0, what is the maximum number of nodes at level 4?
e: The maximum number of nodes at level $L$ (root at level 0) is $2^L$.
Note that 31 is the <u>total</u> number of nodes in levels 0 to 4 ($2^5 - 1$), not the count at level 4 alone.
<mark>16 nodes</mark>

qs.q: What is the minimum possible height of a binary tree that contains 10 nodes? (Height is counted in edges.)
e: A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^{h+1} - 1$ nodes.
Height 2 allows at most $2^3 - 1 = 7$ nodes, which is not enough for 10.
Height 3 allows at most $2^4 - 1 = 15$ nodes, which is enough.
Formula check: $\lceil \log_2(10 + 1) \rceil - 1 = \lceil 3.46 \rceil - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3$.
<mark>Minimum height = 3</mark>

qs.q: Consider this tree (parent → children): `A` → `B`, `C` `B` → `D`, `E` `C` → `F` Which pair of nodes are siblings?
qs.e: Siblings are nodes that have the same parent. `D` and `E` are both children of `B`, so D and E are siblings. `D` and `F` have different parents, and `B` is the parent of `D`.

qs.q: Consider this tree (parent → children): `A` → `B`, `C`, `D` `B` → `E`, `F` `D` → `G` All other nodes are leaves. How many internal nodes and how many leaf nodes does it have?
e: A leaf has no children; an internal node has at least one child.
Internal nodes: `A` (3 children), `B` (2 children), `D` (1 child), so there are 3.
Leaf nodes: `C`, `E`, `F`, `G`, so there are 4.
<mark>3 internal nodes and 4 leaf nodes</mark>

qs.q: Consider this tree (parent → children): `A` → `B`, `C` `B` → `D`, `E` `E` → `F` Which nodes form the subtree rooted at `B`?
qs.e: A subtree is formed by a node <u>and</u> all of its descendants. The descendants of `B` are `D`, `E`, `F`, so the subtree is <mark>B, D, E, F</mark> (`C` belongs to the other branch).

qs.q: Consider this tree (parent → children): `A` → `B`, `C` `B` → `D`, `E` `E` → `F` What is the length of the path `A` → `B` → `E` → `F`?
qs.e: The length of a path is the number of edges on it, not the number of nodes. The path has 4 nodes and 3 edges (`A`-`B`, `B`-`E`, `E`-`F`), so its length is 3.

qs.q: Consider this tree (parent → children): `A` → `B`, `C` `B` → `D`, `E` `E` → `F` How many descendants does node `A` have?
qs.e: The descendants of a node are all nodes below it: `B`, `C`, `D`, `E`, `F`, so there are <mark>5</mark>. The node `A` itself is not counted.

qs.q: What is the height of a leaf node?

c.x: Equal to the height of the tree

qs.e: A leaf has no children, so the longest path from it down to a leaf has no edges. The height of a leaf node is <mark>0</mark>.

qs.q: Which type of binary tree is shown below? Choose the most specific correct description. Tree (parent → left child, right child): `10` → `5`, `15` `5` → `3`, `7` `15` → `12`, `18` All other nodes are leaves.
e: Every internal node (`10`, `5`, `15`) has exactly two children.
All leaves (`3`, `7`, `12`, `18`) are at the same level (level 2).
So the tree is full, complete and balanced, but the most specific description is perfect, which implies the others.
Check: height 2 gives $2^3 - 1 = 7$ nodes, and the tree has exactly 7 nodes.
<mark>Perfect Binary Tree</mark>

qs.q: Which type of binary tree is shown below? Choose the most specific correct description. Tree (parent → left child, right child): `8` → `4`, `12` `4` → `2`, `6` `12` → right child `14` only (no left child) All other nodes are leaves.
e: Full? No: `12` has only one child.
Complete? No: `12` has a right child but no left child, so the last level is not filled from left to right.
Degenerate? No: the root `8` has two children.
BST? Yes: the left subtree `{4, 2, 6}` is smaller than `8`, the right subtree `{12, 14}` is larger than `8`, `2` is less than `4` which is less than `6`, and `14` is greater than `12`.
<mark>Binary Search Tree</mark>

qs.q: Which type of binary tree is shown below? Choose the most specific correct description. Tree (parent → left child, right child): `1` → `2`, `5` `2` → left child `3` only (no right child) All other nodes are leaves.
e: Full? No: `2` has only one child.
Degenerate or skewed? No: the root `1` has two children, so not every node has a single child.
Complete? Yes: levels 0 and 1 are completely filled, and the last level contains only `3`, in the leftmost position.
<mark>Complete Binary Tree</mark>

qs.q: Which type of binary tree is shown below? Choose the most specific correct description. Tree (each node is the left child of its parent): `20` → left child `15` only `15` → left child `10` only `10` → left child `5` only
e: Every internal node has exactly one child, so the tree is degenerate (it behaves like a linked list).
Every child is a left child, so it is more specifically left-skewed.
It is not full, because full trees allow only 0 or 2 children per node.
<mark>Left-Skewed Binary Tree</mark>

qs.q: Which type of binary tree is shown below? Choose the most specific correct description. Tree (parent → left child, right child): `50` → `30`, `70` `30` → `20`, `60` `70` → `40`, `80` All other nodes are leaves.
e: Every internal node has two children and all leaves (`20`, `60`, `40`, `80`) are at level 2, so the tree is perfect (it is also full and complete).
BST check: `60` is in the left subtree of `50` but is greater than `50`, and `40` is in the right subtree of `50` but is smaller than `50`.
So the tree is <u>not</u> a BST, even though its values look ordered.
<mark>Perfect Binary Tree</mark>

qs.q: Which type of binary tree is shown below? Choose the most specific correct description. Tree (parent → left child, right child): `10` → `5`, `15` `5` → `2`, `6` `15` → right child `20` only (no left child) All other nodes are leaves.
e: Full? No: `15` has only one child.
Complete? No: `15` has a right child but no left child.
Perfect? No: not every internal node has two children.
BST? Yes: left subtree `{5, 2, 6}` is smaller than `10`, right subtree `{15, 20}` is larger than `10`, `2` is less than `5` which is less than `6`, and `20` is greater than `15`.
<mark>Binary Search Tree</mark>

qs.q: Which type of binary tree is shown below? Choose the most specific correct description. Tree (parent → left child, right child): `1` → `2`, `5` `2` → `3`, `4` `5` → left child `6` only (no right child) All other nodes are leaves.
e: Levels 0 and 1 are completely filled (`1`; `2`, `5`).
The last level contains `3`, `4`, `6`, filled from left to right with no gap, so the tree is complete.
Full? No: `5` has only one child. Perfect? No: the last level is not full. Degenerate? No: the root has two children.
<mark>Complete Binary Tree</mark>

qs.q: Which type of binary tree is shown below? Choose the most specific correct description. Tree (parent → left child, right child): `50` → `30`, `70` `30` → right child `40` only (no left child) `70` → right child `80` only (no left child) All other nodes are leaves.
e: Degenerate? No: the root has two children.
Perfect? No: `30` and `70` have only one child each.
Complete? No: `30` has a right child but no left child.
BST? Yes: `40` is greater than `30` and smaller than `50`; `80` is greater than `70`, and the whole right subtree is larger than `50`.
<mark>Binary Search Tree</mark>

qs.q: Consider this BST (parent → left child, right child): `50` → `30`, `70` `30` → `20`, `40` `70` → `60`, `80` What is its preorder traversal?
e: Preorder rule: Root → Left → Right.
Visit the root `50`.
Traverse the left subtree of `30`: visit `30`, then `20`, then `40`.
Traverse the right subtree of `70`: visit `70`, then `60`, then `80`.
<mark>Preorder: 50 30 20 40 70 60 80</mark>

qs.q: Consider this BST (parent → left child, right child): `50` → `30`, `70` `30` → `20`, `40` `70` → `60`, `80` What is its inorder traversal?
e: Inorder rule: Left → Root → Right.
Left subtree of `50` gives `20 30 40`.
Then the root `50`.
Right subtree of `50` gives `60 70 80`.
<mark>Inorder: 20 30 40 50 60 70 80</mark> (sorted, as expected for a BST)

qs.q: Consider this BST (parent → left child, right child): `50` → `30`, `70` `30` → `20`, `40` `70` → `60`, `80` What is its postorder traversal?
e: Postorder rule: Left → Right → Root.
Left subtree of `50`: `20`, `40`, then its root `30`.
Right subtree of `50`: `60`, `80`, then its root `70`.
Finally the root `50`.
<mark>Postorder: 20 40 30 60 80 70 50</mark>

qs.q: Consider this BST (parent → left child, right child): `50` → `30`, `70` `30` → `20`, `40` `70` → `60`, `80` What is its level-order traversal?
e: Level-order visits the nodes level by level, from left to right.
<mark>Level-order: 50 30 70 20 40 60 80</mark>

qs.q: Consider this binary tree (parent → left child, right child). It is not a BST: `1` → `2`, `3` `2` → right child `4` only (no left child) `3` → left child `5` only (no right child) All other nodes are leaves. What is its inorder traversal?
e: Inorder rule: Left → Root → Right.
Left subtree of `1` (rooted at `2`): `2` has no left child, so visit `2`, then its right child `4`, giving `2 4`.
Visit the root `1`.
Right subtree of `1` (rooted at `3`): visit the left child `5` first, then `3`, giving `5 3`.
<mark>Inorder: 2 4 1 5 3</mark>

qs.q: Which task is a typical application of preorder traversal?

c.x: Listing the keys of a BST in sorted order

qs.e: Preorder (Root → Left → Right) visits a node before its children, which suits copying a tree, prefix expression generation and serializing a tree. Evaluating expression trees and deleting a tree use postorder, and sorted listing of a BST uses inorder.

qs.q: The inorder traversal of a binary tree is `10 20 15 30`. What can we conclude?

c.x: It is a BST, because inorder traversal always visits nodes from left to right
It is not a BST, because the inorder traversal of a BST must be sorted
It is a BST only if its root holds the key 10
Nothing, because inorder and preorder give the same order for a BST

qs.e: For a BST, inorder traversal visits the keys in ascending sorted order. Here `20` comes before `15`, so the tree cannot be a BST.

qs.q: Which traversal is the most suitable for deleting an entire binary tree?
qs.e: Postorder (Left → Right → Root) processes both children before their parent, which is exactly what deleting a tree needs. Preorder, in contrast, suits copying or serializing a tree.

qs.q: Level-order traversal visits nodes level by level. Which data structure does it generally use to hold the nodes waiting to be visited?
qs.e: The algorithm dequeues a node, visits it, and then enqueues its left and right children. This first-in, first-out order visits nodes level by level, so a <mark>queue</mark> is used.

qs.q: Consider this BST (parent → left child, right child): `50` → `30`, `70` `30` → `20`, `40` `70` → `60`, `80` Which path is followed when searching for 80?
e: Compare `80` with the root `50`: it is greater, so move right to `70`.
Compare `80` with `70`: it is greater, so move right to `80`.
`80` equals the current node, so the search succeeds.
<mark>Path: 50 → 70 → 80</mark>

qs.q: Consider this BST (parent → left child, right child): `50` → `30`, `70` `30` → `20`, `40` `70` → `60`, `80` What happens when searching for 25?

c.x: The path 50, 30, 40 ends at NULL, so 25 is not in the tree
The path 50, 30, 20 ends at 25, so 25 is found as a child of 20
The path 50, 70, 60 ends at NULL, so 25 is not in the tree
The path 50, 30, 20 ends at NULL, so 25 is not in the tree

e: Compare `25` with `50`: it is smaller, so move left to `30`.
Compare `25` with `30`: it is smaller, so move left to `20`.
Compare `25` with `20`: it is greater, so move right, but `20` has no right child (NULL).
<mark>The path 50 → 30 → 20 → NULL shows that 25 does not exist in the tree</mark>

qs.q:
Consider this BST (parent → left child, right child):
`50` → `30`, `70`
`30` → `20`, `40`
`70` → `60`, `80`
The value `65` is inserted. Where is it placed?
e: Start at the root: `65` is greater than `50`, so move right to `70`.
`65` is smaller than `70`, so move left to `60`.
`65` is greater than `60`, so move right; `60` has no right child, so this is an empty position.
<mark>65 becomes the right child of 60</mark>

qs.q: In this BST, `50` has left child `30` and right child `70`, and both `30` and `70` are leaves. The leaf `30` is deleted. What does the tree look like afterwards?

c.x: `70` becomes the root, with `50` as its left child
`50` has a right child `70`, whose left child is `30`

qs.e: Deleting a leaf (Case 1) is simple: just remove the node, since it has no children. `70` stays where it is, so `50` keeps only its right child `70`.

qs.q: In this BST, `50` has only a left child `30`, and `30` has only a right child `40` (`40` is a leaf). The node `30` is deleted. What does the tree look like afterwards?

c.x: `30` stays in the tree and `40` is removed

qs.e: Deleting a node with one child (Case 2): its child takes its place. `40` replaces `30`, so `40` becomes the left child of `50` (it is still smaller than `50`, so the BST property holds).

qs.q: In this BST, `50` has left child `30` and right child `70`; `70` has left child `60` and right child `80` (`30`, `60` and `80` are leaves). The node `70` is deleted and replaced by its inorder successor. What does the tree look like afterwards?

c.x: `50` has left child `30` and right child `60`; `60` has only a right child `80`
`50` has left child `30` and right child `80`; `80` has only a left child `60`
`50` has left child `30` and right child `80`; `80` has left child `60` and right child `80`
`50` has left child `30` and right child `80`; `80` has only a right child `60`

e: `70` has two children (Case 3), so it is replaced by its inorder successor: the smallest value in its right subtree.
The right subtree of `70` is just `80`, so the successor is `80`.
Put `80` in the position of `70`, and delete the original leaf `80` (a Case 1 deletion), so `80` appears only once.
The new `80` keeps the old left child `60` of `70`.
Check: the inorder traversal `30 50 60 80` is still sorted, so it is a valid BST. (Using the predecessor `60` instead would give option 1.)
<mark>50 has left child 30 and right child 80; 80 has only a left child 60</mark>
